question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man arrived to the urgent care pod in the early afternoon stating that his right lower limb had become “one size larger” over the preceding two days, making it difficult to slide into his work trousers this morning. He works as a city bus driver and had completed three consecutive double shifts earlier in the week, each involving long stretches of sitting punctuated by short walks to the depot lounge; afterward he noticed a vague heaviness in the posterior thigh that he dismissed as fatigue from climbing the yard’s metal stairs. When he awoke yesterday the fullness had spread from groin to ankle, and by last night the leg felt heavy enough that stepping onto the brake pedal required conscious effort. He denies stumbling, twisting injuries, insect bites, rashes, or contact with individuals who have cellulitis. There has been no fever, chills, night sweats, malaise, or change in appetite, and he specifically notes no shortness of breath, pleuritic discomfort, hemoptysis, palpitations, or syncope. His past medical history is notable only for diet-controlled dyslipidemia discovered at a screening fair; he takes 20 mg atorvastatin nightly but no other prescription or over-the-counter drugs, herbal products, or hormonal agents. He recalls no prior episodes of leg swelling, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, or stroke, and has never received anticoagulants. There is no personal or familial record of thrombophilia, connective-tissue disease, malignancy, or chronic kidney, liver, or heart disease. He has never undergone chemotherapy or radiation, and his last hospital stay was a same-day colonoscopy five years ago. He denies any neurologic illness, limb weakness, spinal cord injury, or placement of a cast, boot, or splint. He walks his dog three blocks nightly, has not been confined to bed, and completed a three-hour non-stop flight to visit his sister six months earlier without issue. He quit cigarette smoking ten years ago after a 15 pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of red wine with dinner twice weekly, and denies illicit drug use. On arrival he sat upright, conversed easily, and ambulated to the exam table without assistance though favoring the right side. Initial vital signs obtained prior to any medication were temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Cardiac examination disclosed a normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear bilaterally. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities demonstrated striking asymmetry: the entire right limb from proximal thigh to dorsal foot appeared enlarged with a smooth, slightly tense cutaneous surface, while the left maintained normal contour. A flexible tape measure placed 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 42.3 cm on the right and 38.0 cm on the left, a difference of 4.3 cm; 15 cm proximal to the superior patellar border measured 57 cm on the right versus 51 cm on the left. No cord-like subcutaneous veins, varicosities, or spider angiomas were visible, and the skin displayed normal pink coloration without erythema, hyperpigmentation, or ulceration. Gentle thumb pressure over the anterior tibia of the symptomatic limb produced a 3-mm depression that slowly refilled over approximately 20 seconds, whereas identical pressure on the contralateral side left no trace. Temperature of both calves felt similar to the dorsal surface of the examiner’s hand, and there was no overt tenderness when palpating along the femoral triangle, adductor canal, popliteal fossa, or posterior tibial groove; the patient instead described only a dull sense of tightness when the soft tissues were compressed. Passive range of motion at the hip, knee, and ankle was full and pain-free, and the ankle dorsiflexion test did not reproduce sharp discomfort. Distal perfusion was intact with posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally and capillary refill under two seconds in all toes; motor strength was graded 5/5 and sensation to light touch and vibration remained symmetric. There was no inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy and no masses in the groin region. A point-of-care urinalysis showed no proteinuria or hematuria. Baseline laboratory studies drawn before any antithrombotic therapy revealed hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, platelet count 255 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.6 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 19 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 seconds. An electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Plain radiographs of the femur and tibia obtained by the referring urgent care physician earlier in the morning showed only diffuse soft-tissue prominence with intact cortical margins. Given the acute, unilateral, full-length swelling accompanied by a measured calf circumference discrepancy exceeding 3 cm, the demonstration of pitting isolated to the affected leg, the absence of conspicuous superficial venous collaterals, and the lack of a recent musculoskeletal injury, infection, neurologic deficit, or neoplasm that would better account for these findings, vascular imaging of the right lower extremity has been arranged on an expedited basis while laboratory values are finalized and the patient remains under observation.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Wells score for DVT at presentation: add 1 point per positive clinical criterion and subtract 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
- Entire leg swollen: enlargement extends from the right proximal thigh to the foot → +1.
- Calf circumference difference ≥3 cm at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 42.3 − 38.0 = 4.3 cm → +1.
- Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg: right-sided pitting only → +1.
- Localized deep venous tenderness: absent; tightness alone does not qualify → 0.
- Nonvaricose superficial collateral veins: none visible → 0.
- Leg paralysis, paresis, or recent cast immobilization: none → 0.
- Bed rest for ≥3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks: neither; prolonged sitting while driving is not bed rest → 0.
- Active cancer: none → 0.
- Prior DVT: none reported → 0.
- Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT: none identified → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
